title: iPhone 18 Pro Max vs Galaxy S26 Ultra: the full comparison

scenes.text: The newest iPhone Pro Max and the newest Galaxy Ultra both start at about $1,300. So which one is actually better? I went through the official specs, the reviewers' lab tests, and the problems owners are reporting. Here is everything, in ten minutes.
scenes.say: The newest eye phone Pro Max and the newest Galaxy Ultra both start at about thirteen hundred dollars. So which one is actually better? I went through the official specs, the reviewers' lab tests, and the problems owners are reporting. Here is everything, in ten minutes.

scenes.text: Meet the two phones. The iPhone 18 Pro Max went on sale on September 18th, 2026. It runs Apple's new A20 Pro chip. The Galaxy S26 Ultra is Samsung's top phone. It runs a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, and it went on sale on March 11th, about six months earlier. That matters, because the Galaxy has had more time in owners' hands, so more of its problems have been reported. Both are big slab phones with 6.9-inch screens. I left out the foldables, because they are a different kind of phone.

scenes.text: Start with the body. Both screens measure 6.9 inches, and both phones are rated IP68 for dust and water. But the iPhone is the heavier phone: 249 grams, against 214 for the Galaxy. It is also thicker, at 8.75 millimeters, against 7.9. It is the heaviest iPhone Apple has ever made, 16 grams more than last year's Pro Max. Both frames are aluminum. Apple adds Ceramic Shield 2 glass and built-in magnets for MagSafe. Samsung still builds the S Pen stylus into the phone, and the iPhone has no stylus at all. TechRadar also notes a difference in water depth ratings: six meters for the iPhone, one and a half for the Galaxy.

scenes.text: Now the screens. Both are 6.9 inches, and both go up to 120 hertz. The Galaxy has more pixels: 3,120 by 1,440, about 500 pixels per inch, against 2,868 by 1,320 and 460 on the iPhone. For brightness, Apple claims 3,000 nits outdoors, and Samsung claims 2,600. In Tom's Guide's lab, the iPhone measured about 2,300 nits, and the Galaxy about 1,800. But the Galaxy has a feature no iPhone offers: a built-in Privacy Display, which hides the screen from people looking from the side. Android Central says it costs some effective resolution, brightness and contrast. Tom's Guide still gave the display round to Samsung.

scenes.text: Performance is where the gap is clearest. In Geekbench 6, the iPhone scored 4,741 on one core, and 12,789 on all cores. The Galaxy scored 3,785 and 11,563. That makes the iPhone 25 percent faster on one core, and about 11 percent faster on all cores. In the 3DMark Solar Bay graphics test, the iPhone averaged 68 frames per second, and the Galaxy 49. Then a stress test, which shows how much speed each phone keeps when it heats up. The iPhone kept 79 percent of its peak. The Galaxy kept 54. Apple says the vapor chamber in the 18 Pro has three times the surface area of last year's. Both chips are big jumps over last year. 9to5Mac measured the A20 Pro between 22 and 27 percent faster on the processor, and between 40 and 45 percent faster on graphics, than the A19 Pro. Samsung claims 19 percent more processor speed, 24 percent more graphics speed, and 39 percent more on the AI engine, over the S25 Ultra. The Galaxy wins one test, though: Geekbench AI, by about 15 percent.

scenes.text: Now the cameras. The iPhone has three 48 megapixel rear cameras: a main camera with a variable aperture, an ultrawide, and a 4x telephoto. The Galaxy has a 200 megapixel main camera, a 50 megapixel ultrawide, and two telephotos, 3x and 5x. On the front, the iPhone has an 18 megapixel selfie camera, the Galaxy 12. Samsung offers up to 100x digital zoom, Apple up to 40x. The iPhone's main camera can change its aperture, from f/1.48 to f/4.0. In Tom's Guide's tests, the iPhone did better in low light, and the Galaxy read small text better at 40x zoom. At 10x, the detail was remarkably similar. Then the lab scores. DXOMARK tested the iPhone 18 Pro, which has the same cameras as the Pro Max. It scored 172 overall, and 176 for video, the highest video score in its ranking. The Galaxy S26 Ultra scored 157 overall, and 153 for video. One lab is not the final word, but that gap is large.

scenes.text: Battery. The iPhone has the bigger one. Apple does not publish the capacity, but reviewers list 5,391 milliamp hours, against 5,000 for the Galaxy. In Tom's Guide's battery test, the iPhone lasted 18 hours and 27 minutes, and the Galaxy 16 hours and 40. Charging is closer. Both are rated for 60 watts wired and 25 watts wireless. Android Central measured how much each phone charged in 15 minutes: 50 percent for the iPhone, 41 for the Galaxy. In Tom's Guide's test, after 30 minutes the iPhone reached 80 percent, and the Galaxy 77. One difference: only the iPhone has magnets built in.

scenes.text: Software and AI. The iPhone runs iOS 27, with the new Siri AI in beta. Tom's Guide found it less capable than Google's Gemini or ChatGPT's voice mode. The Galaxy runs Samsung's One UI with Gemini built in, plus extras like DeX, for a desktop mode, and Good Lock, for customization. For updates, Samsung promises seven major Android upgrades and seven years of security patches. Apple has not published a number of years for the iPhone 18 line. BGR estimates five to six. Tom's Guide gave this round to Samsung.

scenes.text: Price. Both phones start at about 1,300 dollars, for 256 gigabytes. The iPhone went up 100 dollars from last year. At 512 gigabytes, both cost about 1,500. At one terabyte, the Galaxy is 100 dollars cheaper: 1,800 against 1,900. And only Apple sells a two terabyte model, at 2,500 dollars. These are US launch prices. Your local price and carrier deals will differ.

scenes.text: Now the problems, starting with the iPhone. One is confirmed. On October 3rd, Apple confirmed that some iPhone 18 Pro Max phones lose cellular service on AT&T. Apple said affected phones need a hardware replacement, and that a software update can only prevent it. Others are not confirmed. Some iPhone 18 Pro owners report freezes and restarts linked to Face ID and touch input, and some report crackling audio. Macworld says it could not confirm the Face ID cause, and Apple has not acknowledged the audio reports. Reviews add weaknesses of their own: the heaviest iPhone ever, a 100 dollar price increase, and mostly incremental upgrades. 9to5Mac says iPhone 17 Pro owners have little reason to upgrade. And in the US, the phone is eSIM only.

scenes.text: Now the Galaxy. The biggest complaint is the Privacy Display. Some owners report fuzzy text, headaches and eye strain. How widespread that is remains unclear. Samsung also apologized after advertising a 10 bit panel, when the display is 8 bit with 10 bit processing. In July, owners reported a red stain on the screen after three or four months. Samsung blamed the Privacy Display in strong light at maximum brightness, and said it can fix it. In April, owners reported blurry photos from the 3x telephoto camera, and Samsung said it was investigating. Android Authority lists wireless charging that often drops to 10 to 15 watts. TechRadar caught Gemini claiming an Uber booking that did not exist. And in October, a One UI 9 bug left some phones stuck during setup after a factory reset. Reviewers also point to the unchanged S Pen, no built-in magnets, and the price.

scenes.text: So which one should you buy? Going by the evidence, the iPhone wins on speed, video, battery life and built-in magnets. The Galaxy wins on weight, screen sharpness, zoom range, the S Pen, and seven years of updates. Choose the iPhone if you want the fastest chip and the best video. Choose the Galaxy if you want a lighter phone, a stylus, and the longest update promise. If you already own last year's iPhone Pro, 9to5Mac says there is little reason to upgrade. One more caution: the iPhone has been on sale for less than two months, so its long-term record is still unwritten. Every number in this video comes from the sources in the description.
